targetSkill: Teach the student to recognize when a passage requires background knowledge (historical context, setting conventions, character-type familiarity, genre expectations) to fully understand, and to activate that schema deliberately before reading rather than passively missing meaning. The student is not memorizing facts; the student is building the metacognitive habit of asking 'what do I already know about this?' before comprehension breaks down.
mustHave: A passage whose core meaning depends on schema the reader brings to it — a historical setting, a genre convention, a character archetype, a cultural context that makes the passage legible

Schema that is discoverable or retrievable — a 9th grade Title I student either already has it, or can activate it via a pre-reading prompt (e.g., 'what do you know about life on a farm in the 1800s?')
Observable signals in the passage that flag the schema requirement — period details, setting-specific vocabulary, character types, genre markers the reader must recognize to orient
A meaningful gap between schema-activated and schema-missing reading — the same passage reads very differently depending on whether the reader brought the right prior knowledge
mustNotHave: Passages that require obscure, specialized, or expert-level schema a 9th grader cannot reasonably access or build in one pre-reading move (e.g., specific Victorian legal procedures, detailed religious doctrine, technical scientific background)
Passages where the schema requirement is so dominant the passage cannot be read at all without hours of context-building — schema must be activatable, not rebuildable
Passages where no schema is required — fully self-contained, fully explained on the page
Paragraphs dominated by dialogue (60%+ quotation marks) where the schema is what characters assume about each other rather than what the author assumes about the reader
Nonfiction biographical or memoir prose about real people's lives
Archaic or heavily poetic prose whose schema requirement is inseparable from parsing difficulty
Passages that require sensitive schema a Title I classroom cannot safely activate (trauma-laden historical events, content requiring counselor support)

tierSignals.tier1: Schema requirement is obvious and familiar. A farmhouse setting, a classic fairy-tale opening, a clear historical period a 9th grader recognizes. Quick schema activation (30 seconds of pre-reading) unlocks the passage.
tierSignals.tier2: Schema requirement is identifiable but requires a specific activation move. A period-specific setting a student knows exists but hasn't thought about, a genre convention the student has seen before but needs to name. Moderate pre-reading (1-2 minutes) unlocks the passage.
tierSignals.tier3: Schema requirement is subtle — the reader must recognize that multiple background elements are at play (historical period + social class + genre convention). Extended pre-reading (3-5 minutes) and explicit schema-activation protocol are required.
